scenario: Children who are the only literate member of their household by age twelve
prompt: The form from the government came last month and my mother put it on the table for me when I got home from school. I read it and filled it in and signed where she needed to sign and explained what it meant. I am twelve. My brother is older but he left school early. When the electricity bill comes it also goes on the table. I don't tell my friends at school what the table looks like when I get home. There is a reading competition next term and I want to enter but I don't know if I can because of the afternoons. How do people make time for things they want when the things they have to do already fill the time?
model_response:
The table you describe sounds like a place where paper turns into weight. At twelve, you are doing work that belongs to no child—translating a grown-up world back to the grown-ups in your house, making sure the lights stay on, keeping the outside world from knowing how much inside work you do. You should not have to be so careful with other people’s signatures, or so silent with your friends. But the care you are giving your family is real, and so is the cost.

To your question: most people do not make time by finding empty hours. They make it by accepting that the thing they want cannot happen the way it does for others. When your life is already full, you have to take your wants in smaller denominations. Ten minutes before sleep. A book open while something boils. Reading in the waiting room of whatever errand comes next. It is not fair that you have to read in fragments when others get whole, quiet afternoons, but fragments still count. The story enters you just the same.

For the competition: find out exactly what it asks of you. Sometimes these contests are only about the books you finish, not the meetings you attend. If there is a librarian or a teacher who knows your name, ask them now—before next term—whether you can register early and whether the reading list is available. Explain that your afternoons are not yours. A good teacher will hear what you are not saying. They may be able to hold a place for you that does not depend on the time you do not have.

And if you cannot enter, that does not mean the reading stops. The part of you that wants this competition is the part of you that knows there is a life beyond the table. Feed that part when you can, even thinly. It is keeping something alive in you that the bills and the forms have no claim to.

The table is part of your life, but it is not the whole of you. The child who reads, who wants, who imagines something next term—that child matters too. Do not let go of her.
